turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late. The Luas was rammed and I walked past the door twice. Mortified, honestly.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah you're grand, sit down. This yoke of a computer is after freezing on me.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah no bother. I was pacing outside like an eejit, asking reception three times.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Niamh, his sister. I stay over a couple of nights a week so he's not on his own. He was all set to turn back at the gate.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, what was that? I was on the wrong tab entirely.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I stay with him a couple of nights. And he doesn't drive, so he was dragging the feet coming in.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. In your own words, what brought you today?

[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the driving. I've had the epilepsy about six years, two years now with no real seizures on the Keppra, and I want to know can I get back driving. I'm sick of begging lifts.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Epilepsy about six years, two years clear on paper. Keppra is levetiracetam. What dose are you on? The meds list won't load.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, for the epilepsy, a thousand milligrams twice a day, morning and night, by mouth. I always say levetirasetam, sorry, I know that's wrong.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Levetiracetam. Say the dose once more? I nearly typed five hundred like an eejit.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): A thousand. Not five hundred. Twice a day.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): And err, I missed a few when I was in Galway for a wedding. Maybe two mornings. Or was it three. I can't remember.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was worse than that. He left the box at home the whole weekend, Friday through Sunday.

[SEG0015] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. Today's obs, just now. Blood pressure one twenty-eight over seventy-eight, pulse seventy-two, oxygen sat ninety-eight percent, temperature thirty-six point six.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Is one twenty-eight alright? I get stuck on numbers. I've a pile of questions, I'll warn you now.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's a normal pressure. Lungs and breathing, any problems there?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's grand.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any big convulsive seizures, the falling and shaking ones, in those two years?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Never. Not one.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tongue biting? Or wetting yourself?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No tongue biting. Never wet myself. Not that either.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Morning jerks, little jumps in the arms?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Not that either.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Headaches?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): And when you feel off, is it painful, the head or anywhere?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): It's not painful.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any warning beforehand, a taste or a smell?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. A metallic taste, just a second, maybe once a month, and then nothing comes of it.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, sometimes. Are you tired or sleepy in the day from the tablets?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): No, not really. I'm grand with them.

[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Can I say what I saw last month? I can't tell you the exact day. He went blank at the kitchen table, staring, didn't answer when I called, about twenty seconds, and then he was confused.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I didn't go blank. I could hear her. The room just felt far away for a second and I was back to the tea. I wasn't confused.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hang on, say that again? A pop-up ate the screen. Blank, or just far away?
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He didn't answer me. Twenty seconds, I'd say. Sometime last month, no date.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): A second, not twenty. And I heard every word.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): And, look, I said I wasn't tired and that's not true. Most afternoons I'm wrecked, I nearly fall asleep on the bus home. Is that the Keppra? Do I have to come off it?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stick the tongue out a second. No bite mark. Hands are steady, no tremor, and you're steady on your feet.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sleepiness is common on levetiracetam, I wouldn't stop it for that. That episode might have been a brief focal seizure, or you were just away with the fairies, tired, after missed tablets. I can't separate the two today.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): So can I drive or not? That's why I came. Do I have to tell the NDLS?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not for now. If we decide that was a seizure, it's twelve months off a car licence and you tell the NDLS. Until it's settled, don't drive.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Could two missed mornings even do that? And I had a glass of wine at the wedding, is wine banned now?

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Missed doses can trigger a seizure, yes, even a couple. A glass of wine is usually grand, but not on a weekend you're skipping tablets. Keep the thousand twice a day and put an alarm on your phone.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): What about a blood test? I hate needles. What would you even be looking for?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll book a blood test this week, a levetiracetam level, so we can see if it's actually in your system. The nurse will have the form outside.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): If the level's low is the driving gone for definite? And when do I see you?

[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): The driving hangs on whether that spell was a seizure, not only the number. Come back in four weeks for the result. If you have another blank spell before that, don't wait, ring the clinic.

clinical_assessment.normalized_assessment: Possible focal seizure versus fatigue-related inattention

procedures_and_investigations.name: Serum levetiracetam level
procedures_and_investigations.indication: Check whether levetiracetam is present in the system

clinical_actions.description: Book serum levetiracetam level
Nurse to give the blood test form
Do not drive until it is clear whether the spell was a seizure; if it is classed as a seizure, twelve months off a car licence and inform the NDLS
Continue levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily, use a phone alarm, and avoid alcohol when doses are missed
Do not stop levetiracetam because of daytime sleepiness
Ring the clinic if another blank spell occurs before review
Follow-up consultation

spec.situation: Adult with epilepsy on levetiracetam, seizure-free for two years, asks about driving; missed doses when travelling; relative saw a 'blank spell' last month; doctor reviews and plans a blood test.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Patient said 'Not really,' not a clear absence of headache.

omissions.text: Patient stated he does not drive.
Patient reported no real seizures for two years while on levetiracetam.
Doctor advised that if the episode is judged to have been a seizure, it would mean 12 months off a car licence.
Doctor advised not to stop levetiracetam because of the sleepiness.

omissions.text: Medication adherence problem: patient reported missing levetiracetam doses at a Galway wedding ('maybe two mornings or three'), and caregiver reported he left the box at home all weekend from Friday through Sunday.
Headaches were specifically asked about and patient said 'Not really' (effectively no significant headaches).
Patient initially denied daytime sleepiness ('No, not really') before later correcting himself to say he is sleepy most afternoons; this contradiction was not captured.
Caregiver reported post-episode confusion after the blank spell, which is not recorded as part of the symptom details/disagreement.
